cf.title: support create index on virtual generated column.

input.subject: support create index on virtual generated column.

verdict_reasoning: The proposal fails at level 1b on already-exists-1 and prior-attempts-1. Message #9 says an expression index already gives the same result and that indexing a virtual column removes the cheap SET EXPRESSION. No message answers it, and the v9 author agreed with it in message #28. Both objections are fixable, since message #15 proposed a narrower version and did not reject the goal. The list must agree on the goal and on one design before code review makes sense.

brief.title: Allow create index on virtual generated columns
brief.problem: Postgres rejects indexes on virtual generated columns, so users must write an expression index with the generation expression instead. Corey Huinker wants queries that move from the expression to the virtual column to keep using the existing index. Tom Lane replied that expression indexes already cover this need.
brief.proposed_design: Jian He's v1 rewrites an index on a virtual generated column into an expression index on the generation expression. It records the source column in a new pg_index column so SET EXPRESSION and SET DATA TYPE rebuild the index. His v8 drops that tracking and just expands the expression at create index, while Zizhuan Liu's v2 to v9 store column values in the index and expand them at plan time.
user_visible_surface: create index accepts a virtual generated column as a key column; v9 also allows it in expressions, INCLUDE and where predicates.
New pg_index column indattrgenerated (int2vector) lists the virtual generated columns an index uses (v1 to v7 only).
alter table ... alter column ... set expression rebuilds dependent indexes (v1 to v7), or leaves them unchanged (v8).
Unique and deferrable unique constraints on virtual generated columns (v9 only).
author_claims: An index on a virtual generated column stores the same pg_index data as the matching expression index, so the planner produces the same plans.
v1 to v7 support all index types: btree, gist, spgist, hash, gin and brin.
v8 is much simpler but must document that SET EXPRESSION does not affect existing indexes.
The DefineIndex() comment saying RelationGetIndexExpressions() needs changes is wrong.
v9 matches stored generated columns in most catalog behavior and passes the regression tests.
brief.thread_state: Kirill Reshke found that v9 corrupts the index after SET EXPRESSION and crashes on a deferred unique constraint, and v9 no longer applies. Zizhuan Liu then said he agrees with Tom Lane that the feature should not be done, and no newer patch or reply follows.
unclear: Nobody says which design, if any, the CommitFest entry now proposes: v1 tracking, v8 plain expansion, or v9 stored-like values.
The thread has no answer to Tom Lane's objection that indexing a virtual column removes the cheap SET EXPRESSION.
The material has no documentation hunk for create index or generated columns telling users how SET EXPRESSION treats indexes.
The thread does not answer Peter Eisentraut's simpler plan to allow virtual columns in expression indexes and block SET EXPRESSION when indexed.
Nobody says how pg_dump shows the index under v8, as the column or as the expanded expression.

objections.title: Expression indexes on the generation expression already meet the stated need
objections.failure_scenario: A user who wants index support for a virtual column writes `create index on example (lower(regular_name))` today. Queries on `lowercase_name` should already use it, because the planner sees the expanded expression. The patch adds a second spelling and permanent catalog, ALTER TABLE and planner code for little gain.
objections.argument: Tom Lane noted in message #9 that this "does nothing you haven't been able to do for decades with expression indexes". Corey's use case in message #11 is queries that move from the expression to the virtual column and still hit the existing index. Virtual columns are expanded to their expression before index matching, so the existing expression index should already serve those queries. Message #10 shows both index forms give the same pg_index data and plans, and Zizhuan Liu accepted Tom's position in message #28.
objections.author_must_show: Which query or workload fails today with an expression index on the generation expression, and how does the patch fix it?

critic.reasoning: Postgres expands virtual generated columns before index matching, so an expression index already serves the queries in message #11. Message #10 shows the same pg_index data and plans, and the thread shows no case that the expression index cannot serve.

objections.title: Tom Lane's objection to the goal has no answer in the thread
objections.failure_scenario: A user indexes a virtual generated column and later runs alter table ... set expression, expecting a cheap catalog change. Under v1 to v7 the command rebuilds the index. Under v8 the index silently keeps the old expression, and under v9 Kirill Reshke found the index corrupted. The user finds out when the command is slow or when a query returns wrong results.
objections.argument: Message #9 objects to the goal itself. The point of a virtual column is that set expression costs nothing, and expression indexes already give the same result. Corey Huinker's migration use case in message #11 is met by the existing expression index, because v1 to v7 store the same pg_index data (message #10). The v9 author agreed with Tom Lane in message #28, and no later message gives a reason the gain outweighs the lost property.
objections.author_must_show: Which users need an index on the virtual column itself rather than an expression index, and which set expression behaviour should they get?

critic.reasoning: No message answers message #9, and message #28 agrees with it. Peter Eisentraut proposed a narrower version in message #15 and did not reject the goal, so a new version could answer this.

other_surviving.title: Under v8, an index created on column b silently stops tracking b
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user runs create index on t (b), then later runs alter table t alter column b set expression as (a * 3). The index stays on (a * 2), so queries on b fall back to a sequential scan. The user finds out from a slow query, and \d and pg_dump show an expression index they never wrote.
other_surviving.argument: Message #16 says v8 stores only the expanded expression and that the docs must say SET EXPRESSION does not affect existing indexes. That gives a column reference in create index a different meaning from the same command on a stored generated column, where the index follows the column. The material has no documentation hunk for this, and no decision on whether \d and pg_dump should show b or the expression. Message #15 proposed blocking SET EXPRESSION while the column is indexed, and the thread has no answer to it.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Why should create index on (b) accept a column name and then drop the link to it, instead of rejecting SET EXPRESSION as message #15 suggests?

critic.reasoning: Message #16 confirms that v8 leaves the index on the old expression after SET EXPRESSION and needs a documentation note. The material has no such note and no reply to the alternative in message #15.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Indexing a virtual column changes what SET EXPRESSION costs
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A DBA's migration runs set expression on a virtual column, expecting a catalog-only change. Under v1 to v7 or v9, an index someone else added on that column forces a rebuild under an exclusive lock on a large table. The DBA finds out when the migration blocks production traffic.
other_surviving.argument: Message #9 says the main property of a virtual column is that its expression can change cheaply, and that an index removes that property. v1 to v7 rebuild the index on SET EXPRESSION (messages #1 and #10), and v9 corrupts it (message #27). No later message answers the objection in message #9. Message #10 asks whether the index should be rebuilt or marked invalid, and the thread never settles it, so this part of the user-facing contract has no defined behaviour.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which SET EXPRESSION behaviour on an indexed virtual column does the proposal commit to, and how do users learn that its cost differs from an unindexed column?

critic.reasoning: A rebuild on its own copies existing practice, since SET DATA TYPE on an indexed column also rebuilds indexes. But the question in message #10 has no answer, so the proposal commits to no SET EXPRESSION behaviour.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Index with stored virtual column values breaks after SET EXPRESSION
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user indexes a virtual column under v9 and later runs alter table ... alter column v set expression. The index keeps entries computed from the old expression while heap reads compute the new one. Index scans return wrong rows on the primary and on every physical standby, and the user finds out only from wrong results or from amcheck.
other_surviving.argument: Message #27 shows this with bt_index_check reporting a heap tuple with no matching index tuple. The v9 design writes values computed from the expression into index tuples, but nothing records that the index depends on the expression. The only safe fix is a forced index rebuild on SET EXPRESSION, which removes the cheap catalog-only change that message #9 names as the point of virtual columns. Message #28 withdraws v9 on these grounds.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How does a stored-value design keep index tuples consistent with the heap after SET EXPRESSION without rebuilding every dependent index?

critic.reasoning: Message #27 shows the corruption with bt_index_check. It applies only to v9, which its author stopped supporting in message #28, and a rebuild on SET EXPRESSION would fix it, so it is fixable.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: v9 needs raw and expanded copies of every index expression
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A later patch reads rd_indexprs or ii_Expressions where it needed the expanded copy, or the reverse. Nothing fails at build time or in the usual tests. Users then find an index that silently disagrees with the heap, as amcheck showed in message #27 after SET EXPRESSION.
other_surviving.argument: Message #18 adds paired raw and expanded fields to IndexInfo, RelationData and IndexOptInfo. The author says choosing between the two copies took most of the effort and needed a spreadsheet audit. Messages #20-#23 also change genericcostestimate() and cost_index() for every index, so costing changes for people who do not use the feature. Message #27 found index corruption and a crash in exactly these paths, and message #28 withdraws support for the design.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What would make a future patch fail loudly if it read the raw index expression where the expanded one was required?

critic.reasoning: Message #18 confirms the paired fields and the audit effort, and messages #20 to #23 confirm the costing changes for all indexes. This applies only to v9, and v1 to v8 avoid it, so it is fixable by choice of design.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Tracking design adds catalog state that every ALTER path must consult
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A future alter table subcommand changes a virtual column but does not check pg_index.indattrgenerated. The dependent index is not rebuilt and keeps entries for the old expression. Users find out from wrong query results or amcheck errors.
other_surviving.argument: v1 to v7 add the int2vector column indattrgenerated and teach tablecmds.c to rebuild indexes on SET EXPRESSION and SET DATA TYPE. Message #2 shows this dependency bookkeeping already went wrong once with drop column. In message #15 Peter Eisentraut proposed a design with no new catalog column, no rebuild, and SET EXPRESSION blocked while the column is indexed. The thread has no answer to that proposal.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Why is a new pg_index column with rebuild logic better than blocking SET EXPRESSION on indexed virtual columns?

critic.reasoning: Message #16 asks how to tell the indexes apart without a catalog column, but does not say why blocking SET EXPRESSION through the dependency added in v2 is not enough. v8 drops the column, so this applies to v1 to v7 only.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: New pg_index column adds dependency state every index path must follow
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch adds an ALTER path that changes a virtual column but does not check indattrgenerated. Dependent indexes are not rebuilt and keep old expression values without any error, and users find the stale index only from wrong query results.
refuted.argument: v1 to v7 add indattrgenerated to pg_index so that SET EXPRESSION and SET DATA TYPE can find indexes to rebuild (message #1). Correctness then depends on every column-changing command checking this column, and nothing fails loudly if one does not. Message #15 suggests blocking SET EXPRESSION when the column is indexed, which needs no new catalog column, and the thread does not answer that suggestion.
refuted.author_must_show: Why is a new pg_index column better than blocking SET EXPRESSION on indexed virtual columns through the existing dependency mechanism?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-2, which makes the same point about indattrgenerated and adds the drop column evidence from message #2.

refuted.title: Indexing virtual columns gives up cheap SET EXPRESSION and adds little
refuted.failure_scenario: Under v8 a user indexes a virtual column and later runs SET EXPRESSION. The index keeps the old expanded expression, and the planner no longer matches it to the column. The index stays, costs writes and is never used, and no message tells the user why.
refuted.argument: Message #9 says the point of a virtual column is a cheap SET EXPRESSION, and that expression indexes already give the same plans. Message #10 confirms the plans are identical. Corey Huinker's migration case in message #11 is met today by an expression index, since the planner expands the virtual column. Whatever SET EXPRESSION semantics the project picks for indexed virtual columns, it cannot change them later.
refuted.author_must_show: Which user query works with an index on the virtual column but not with an expression index on the generation expression?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1 and already-exists-1. The added claim that the chosen semantics can never change has no support in the material.

refuted.title: The v8 form duplicates expression indexes and keeps the old expression
refuted.failure_scenario: A user runs `create index on t (v)`, then `alter table t alter column v set expression as (a * 3)`. Under v8 the index still holds `a * 2`. Queries on `v` stop using the index, and the user learns this only from slower plans or by reading the index definition.
refuted.argument: Message #16 says v8 expands the expression at create index time without tracking, and that the docs must say SET EXPRESSION has no effect on existing indexes. That makes v8 an expression index under a column name, and it can diverge from the column after SET EXPRESSION. Peter Eisentraut's alternative in message #15 keeps the existing mechanism and blocks SET EXPRESSION for indexed columns, which avoids the divergence. The material does not say whether pg_dump emits the column or the expanded expression.
refuted.author_must_show: Why is an index named by the column but frozen to the old expression better than requiring an explicit expression index?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which describes the same v8 behaviour after SET EXPRESSION and the same unanswered alternative from message #15.

refuted.title: The one stated use case already works with an expression index
refuted.failure_scenario: A user adds a virtual column whose expression matches an existing expression index and moves queries to the column. The rewriter expands the column to its expression, so the existing index already matches. The new create index form gives this user nothing, but the project still maintains it.
refuted.argument: Corey Huinker's request in message #11 is the only user need in the thread, and he describes a migration case, not an indexing gap. Message #10 shows that an index on the column and an expression index on lower(regular_name) give the same pg_index row and the same plans. That shows the feature is equivalent to the workaround, so it does not show a need for it. Tom Lane made the same point in message #9, and in message #28 the v9 author agreed. No -general or -bugs report and no production case appears in the material.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users today cannot get the plan they need with an expression index on the generation expression, and what do they do instead?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1, which makes the same point from messages #9, #10 and #11.

refuted.title: The gain is syntax, and it removes the cheap set expression
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA indexes a virtual column for convenience, then runs alter table ... set expression and expects an instant catalog change. Under v1 to v7 the index is rebuilt. Under v8 it keeps the old expression without a warning. Under v9 it was corrupted in message #27.
refuted.argument: Tom Lane noted in message #9 that a changeable expression with no stored data is the main reason to choose a virtual column. Every version gives up part of that, or adds catalog state such as indattrgenerated to keep it, and the only gain is not writing the expression in create index. Peter Eisentraut's narrower plan in message #15, which blocks set expression when the column is indexed, has no reply in the thread.
refuted.author_must_show: What benefit over an expression index justifies losing the free set expression, and why is Peter Eisentraut's restricted version not enough?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1. Item 4 also fits poorly, because only users who index the virtual column pay the SET EXPRESSION cost.

Which design does the CommitFest entry now propose: v1 to v7 tracking, v8 plain expansion, or v9 stored values?
What does alter table ... set expression do to an indexed virtual column: rebuild the index, mark it invalid, leave it unchanged, or raise an error?

committability.owner_note: Tom Lane objected to the goal in message #9 and Peter Eisentraut proposed a narrower scope in message #15; neither supports the current patches. An owner would need to know generated columns, index DDL and ALTER TABLE.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the SET EXPRESSION and SET DATA TYPE behaviour of indexed virtual columns for good. Under v1 to v7 that includes a pg_index column every later ALTER path must check.
committability.author_follow_up: Jian He posted v1 to v8 and answered review, but no patch or reply follows message #28. The entry has needed a rebase since 2026-10-10.

priority.reason: The thread shows one interested user, and an expression index appears to cover his case. Three incompatible designs are on the table, they touch the catalog, ALTER TABLE and planner code, and the narrower plan in message #15 has no answer.

precedents_retrieved.title: generated columns
precedents_retrieved.summary: Peter Eisentraut proposed implementing SQL-standard generated columns (GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr)), with the generation expression stored in pg_attrdef like a default and MySQL/Oracle-style VIRTUAL|STORED syntax. Only the VIRTUAL (computed-on-read) variant was fully implemented; STORED, various ALTER TABLE forms and index support were deferred.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Review by Jaime Casanova found multiple bugs: generated columns showed no value through a view, inheritance produced a malformed default and a server crash on insert, ALTER COLUMN TYPE on the referenced or generated column failed with internal errors, triggers saw NULL for the generated column, and the generation expression could be dropped via DROP DEFAULT. Based on these reviews, the commitfest manager marked the entry Returned with feedback, asking for an updated version to be resubmitted.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow logical decoding to output generated columns
precedents_retrieved.authors: Peter Smith (smithpb2250), Shubham Khanna (skhanna), Shlok Kyal (shlokkyal)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Let pgoutput send generated column values in logical replication, so consumers get a complete row instead of computing generated columns on the subscriber. The work added replication of generated columns named in a publication column list, then a publish_generated_columns publication parameter.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Most of the work was committed before the entry closed: generated columns in column lists and the publish_generated_columns parameter. After that commit, Peter Eisentraut asked how the feature should work with the proposed virtual generated columns, which he thought could not be replicated, and Amit Kapila suggested limiting the option to stored generated columns. The thread then went idle in Waiting on Author, and Michael Paquier returned the entry until that question is settled.

precedents_retrieved.title: Change tuple table slot for Unique node to "virtual"
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Heikki Linnakangas, David Rowley, Ashutosh Bapat
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changed the Unique node's result slot from a minimal tuple slot to a virtual slot, because the copy into a minimal tuple slot (with palloc) made DISTINCT slower than the equivalent GROUP BY. A later version used the outer child's slot type instead of a fixed type.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Benchmarks showed mixed results. Heikki Linnakangas found a slowdown when the input is a minimal tuple from a Sort, and David Rowley measured Q2 and Q3 as slower with the revised patch because tts_virtual_materialize() costs more. Ashutosh Bapat doubted the change was worth pursuing when only one query improved clearly. The author then asked how slot types should be chosen across all materialization nodes, and the entry was withdrawn after an offline discussion.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Q1 is consistently giving performance > 25% for both of us. But other queries aren't showing a whole lot improvement.

precedents_retrieved.title: doc: virtual envs with Pl/Python
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a note to the PL/Python documentation on using a Python virtual environment, so that extra packages do not have to be installed into the system interpreter. The note points to the environment variables PL/Python already honors.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the docs should not teach Python, and that the patch describes one installation pattern that may not apply on every platform. He and Jacob Champion added that a virtualenv user already knows about PYTHONPATH, and that the patch does not say how to set it for the server, which varies by packaging. Jacob Champion found the text too prescriptive and suggested a wiki page that also lists alternatives. The author withdrew the entry.

More, this
patch seems like not merely teaching Python, but teaching the use of

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove useless GROUP BY columns considering unique index
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets remove_useless_groupby_columns use unique constraints whose columns are all NOT NULL, in addition to the primary key, to drop functionally dependent GROUP BY columns. When several candidates exist, it picks the one with the fewest columns so that the most columns can be removed.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch no longer applied because it relied on catalogued NOT NULL constraints, which had been removed. David Rowley also objected to choosing the constraint with the fewest columns, which ignores column width and can pick a constraint with no columns in the GROUP BY clause, a regression against today's primary-key behaviour. The author said he would study the advice and update, but the visible messages show no new version before the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It looks like it  won't work if the UNIQUE constraint with
the least columns gets no mention in the GROUP BY clause. That'll
cause performance regressions from what we have today when the primary
key is mentioned and columns can be removed using that but a UNIQUE
constraint exists which has no corresponding GROUP BY columns and
fewer unique columns than the PK.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improving default column names/aliases of subscript text expressions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the default column name for a subscript expression with a string-literal subscript, such as data['a'] on jsonb, to the subscript value instead of the base column name. A later POC derives the name from the transformed expression and leaves room for type-specific hooks, so subscript implementations could supply their own default alias.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that changing default column names breaks existing queries, and that a GUC to switch the behavior would change query semantics. He was not convinced the new names were better, preferring names like "data_a" if anything changed. He called the transformed-expression POC a single-purpose kluge and suggested that extensible field selection would serve the author's use case better.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
Reverted commit(s): Ensure that RowExprs and whole-row Vars produce the expected column names.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
In commit bf7ca1587, I had the bright idea that we could make the
result of a whole-row Var (that is, foo.*) track any column aliases
that had been applied to the FROM entry the Var refers to.  However,
that's not terribly logically consistent, because now the output of
the Var is no longer of the named composite type that the Var claims
to emit.  bf7ca1587 tried to handle that by changing the output
tuple values to be labeled with a blessed RECORD type, but that's
really pretty disastrous: we can wind up storing such tuples onto
disk, whereupon they're not readable by other sessions.

The only practical fix I can see is to give up on what bf7ca1587
tried to do, and say that the column names of tuples produced by
a whole-row Var are always those of the underlying named composite
type, query aliases or no.  While this introduces some inconsistencies,
it removes others, so it's not that awful in the abstract.  What *is*
kind of awful is to make such a behavioral change in a back-patched
bug fix.  But corrupt data is worse, so back-patched it will be.

(A workaround available to anyone who's unhappy about this is to
introduce an extra level of sub-SELECT, so that the whole-row Var is
referring to the sub-SELECT's output and not to a named table type.
Then the Var is of type RECORD to begin with and there's no issue.)

Per report from Miles Delahunty.  The faulty commit dates to 9.5,
so back-patch to all supported branches.

Reverted commit(s): Fix index-only scan plans when not all index columns can be returned.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 4ace45677 failed to fix the problem fully, because the
same issue of attempting to fetch a non-returnable index column
can occur when rechecking the indexqual after using a lossy index
operator.  Moreover, it broke EXPLAIN for such indexquals (which
indicates a gap in our test cases :-().

Revert the code changes of 4ace45677 in favor of adding a new field
to struct IndexOnlyScan, containing a version of the indexqual that
can be executed against the index-returned tuple without using any
non-returnable columns.  (The restrictions imposed by check_index_only
guarantee this is possible, although we may have to recompute indexed
expressions.)  Support construction of that during setrefs.c
processing by marking IndexOnlyScan.indextlist entries as resjunk
if they can't be returned, rather than removing them entirely.
(We could alternatively require setrefs.c to look up the IndexOptInfo
again, but abusing resjunk this way seems like a reasonably safe way
to avoid needing to do that.)

This solution isn't great from an API-stability standpoint: if there
are any extensions out there that build IndexOnlyScan structs directly,
they'll be broken in the next minor releases.  However, only a very
invasive extension would be likely to do such a thing.  There's no
change in the Path representation, so typical planner extensions
shouldn't have a problem.

As before, back-patch to all supported branches.

precedents_retrieved.summary:
Relax transactional restrictions on ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE (redux).
Reverted commit(s): Revert to 9.6 treatment of ALTER TYPE enumtype ADD VALUE.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Originally committed as 15bc038f (plus some follow-ups), this was
reverted in 28e07270 due to a problem discovered in parallel
workers.  This new version corrects that problem by sending the
list of uncommitted enum values to parallel workers.

Here follows the original commit message describing the change:

To prevent possibly breaking indexes on enum columns, we must keep
uncommitted enum values from getting stored in tables, unless we
can be sure that any such column is new in the current transaction.

Formerly, we enforced this by disallowing ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE
from being executed at all in a transaction block, unless the target
enum type had been created in the current transaction.  This patch
removes that restriction, and instead insists that an uncommitted enum
value can't be referenced unless it belongs to an enum type created
in the same transaction as the value.  Per discussion, this should be
a bit less onerous.  It does require each function that could possibly
return a new enum value to SQL operations to check this restriction,
but there aren't so many of those that this seems unmaintainable.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent matches. [P2] is the original generated columns patch, returned for bugs in the base feature, and that reason does not apply here. Message #18 links to earlier threads and CommitFest entries, and message #25 mentions CF6749, but the material gives no recorded outcome for them.
Not applicable; two objections raised. v9's unique and deferrable constraints were not judged separately, because its reviewer withdrew support in message #28.
v8 stores only a plain expression index and adds no persistent state beyond what expression indexes have today, so this angle finds nothing in it.

No security or privilege objection at the level of the idea or design. Every variant ends up with an index whose expressions are built from the generation expression. Postgres already evaluates such expressions in expression indexes, under the same owner and security-restricted rules during REINDEX, VACUUM and ANALYZE. The deferred unique constraint crash in v9 (message #27) is an implementation defect, and the v9 author has stepped back from that version (message #28).
Committability: no committer supports the feature in the thread. Tom Lane is against it and Peter Eisentraut proposed a narrower scope. The v9 reviewer withdrew support in message #28.
Two objections. The precedent [P2] is about generated columns themselves and does not apply.
Two objections are raised. The material shows one interested user, and his case looks already covered by expression indexes.
